meta.title: Who really said "Live as if you were to die tomorrow. Learn as if you were to live forever"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Gandhi. The maxim was in print in 1867 — two years before his birth — credited to St Edmund of Abingdon as advice to his Oxford pupils.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Live as if you were to die tomorrow. Learn as if you were to live forever'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Gandhi. Documented in 1867, two years before he was born, as St Edmund of Abingdon's maxim to his Oxford students.

answer.label: Not Mahatma Gandhi — a schoolmaster's maxim in print before he was born
answer.authorDates: c. 1174–1240 · Oxford teacher & Archbishop of Canterbury
answer.sourceLine: Gandhi cannot have originated this: the maxim was already in print in 1867 — two years before his birth — in Augusta Theodosia Drane’s Christian Schools and Scholars, which gives it as the favourite maxim of St Edmund of Abingdon (d. 1240) to his Oxford pupils, worded “Study as if you were to live for ever, live as if you were to die to-morrow.” The attribution to Edmund is a Victorian report of a medieval tradition rather than a documented medieval text, and the modern re-worded, clause-reversed version circulating under Gandhi’s name has no traced author at all.

source.excerpt: As soon as he had taken his master’s degree, he opened a school of his own, on the spot now occupied by St. Edmund’s Hall. The favourite maxim he was accustomed to give to his pupils, was this: ‘Study as if you were to live for ever, live as if you were to die to-morrow.’
trail: 1867 — the decisive date. The maxim is printed on p. 147 of Drane’s Christian Schools and Scholars, vol. II ↗, credited to St Edmund of Abingdon. Gandhi was born in 1869, so the line predates him by two years.

Flagged as a fake Gandhi quote. Gizmodo’s “7 Gandhi Quotes That Are Totally Fake” ↗ lists it, citing the 1867 printing and noting that later-19th-century books credit either the Catholic saint Edmund Rich (d. 1240) or a figure called Ansalus de Insulis.

Listed only as disputed. Wikiquote’s Mahatma Gandhi page ↗ carries this line in its Disputed section, not among his sourced quotes, and points to 19th-century attributions (Edmund Rich, Alain de Lille) rather than any Gandhi source. Quote Investigator has never published an investigation of it — so no specialist has endorsed the Gandhi credit.
The Isidore claim does not survive checking. The popular citation to the Etymologiae, Book III, ch. 24 fails: that book is on the quadrivium ↗ and ch. 24 concerns the name of astronomy.
source.excerptNote: Note the differences from the version that circulates under Gandhi’s name: the clauses run in the opposite order, and the verb is “Study,” not “Learn.” The page number was confirmed from the running head on the scanned leaf, which reads “Old Oxford. 147.”

source.rightsNote: The medieval maxim is ancient and the earliest documented English wording — Drane’s 1867 text ↗ — was published well before 1931 and is in the public domain in the United States. The exact sentence circulated under Gandhi’s name is a different thing: it reverses Drane’s clauses and swaps “Study” for “Learn,” and no author, translator or first printing for that specific rewording has been traced — so we assert no rights status for the popular wording itself.

author.name: St Edmund of Abingdon
author.heading: The man the maxim is traditionally credited to
author.metaLine: c. 1174–1240 · Oxford teacher & Archbishop of Canterbury
author.bio: Edmund of Abingdon (c. 1174–1240) was one of Oxford’s earliest masters of arts, lecturing on mathematics and dialectics, and was reputedly the first to teach Aristotle’s philosophy there. The site where he lived and taught later became St Edmund Hall, still part of the University of Oxford. He was appointed Archbishop of Canterbury in 1233 and consecrated in April 1234, and was canonised soon after his death. The saying is credited to him as a classroom maxim — advice to students — which is exactly the register the line still carries today, long after Gandhi’s name was pinned to it.

misattribution.heading: How the credit went wrong
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “Gandhi” lines on the internet, and one of the easiest to disprove: the date alone settles it. Two rival origin stories also circulate, and one of them is demonstrably false.

items.why: Gandhi was born in 1869. The maxim is already in print in 1867 ↗, which makes him impossible as its origin — a point also made in Gizmodo’s roundup of fake Gandhi quotes ↗. It is credited to him in no documented speech, book or letter, and Wikiquote’s Gandhi page ↗ lists it under Disputed — not among his sourced quotes — recording rival attributions to Isidore of Seville, Edmund Rich and Alain de Lille rather than any Gandhi source.

A widely-copied claim holds that “Disce tamquam semper victurus; vive tamquam cras moriturus” appears in Isidore’s Etymologiae, Book III, ch. 24. It does not. Book III covers the quadrivium ↗ — arithmetic, music, geometry and astronomy — and ch. 24 is on the name of astronomy (De astronomiae nomine). The Latin words victurus and moriturus do not occur in the book at all.

Alongside Edmund Rich, some later-19th-century books credit a figure named Ansalus de Insulis, as Gizmodo notes ↗. The name looks like a garbling of Alanus de Insulis — Alain de Lille (c. 1128–1202/03) — to whom Wikiquote traces the aphorism ↗ via Samuel Smiles’s Duty (1881). We found no primary text in Alain’s own works carrying the maxim, so the chain still ends unverified — but the name is a corruption rather than an invention.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented form is not Gandhi’s and not quite the famous sentence: “Study as if you were to live for ever, live as if you were to die to-morrow” ↗ — a maxim for Oxford students, printed in 1867 and credited to a 13th-century archbishop.

context.heading: A classroom motto, not a mahatma's aphorism
lead: The line reads like advice to a student because that is what it was. Drane’s 1867 history of education sets it in a specific place: Edmund of Abingdon, newly a master of arts, opening “a school of his own, on the spot now occupied by St. Edmund’s Hall” — and handing his pupils a maxim balancing urgency against patience. Learning is a long game; life is not. Hold both at once.

Quite how Gandhi’s name became attached is untraced — and worth saying plainly rather than guessing. What is documented is that he is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for unsourced uplift: Quote Investigator reached much the same verdict on “an eye for an eye makes the whole world blind,” noting the Gandhi family believes it authentic while no example of his using it has ever been found ↗. A memorable thought plus a famous name is a stable compound, and it rarely needs a citation to travel.
detailsBody: 1867 (documented): “Study as if you were to live for ever, live as if you were to die to-morrow.”
Modern (attributed to Gandhi): “Live as if you were to die tomorrow. Learn as if you were to live forever.”

Two changes: the clauses are reversed, putting live first for punch, and “Study” softens to the broader “Learn.” Neither change can be pinned to a datable source, so the popular sentence is best described as an anonymous modern polish of an old maxim.
context.pull: Learning is a long game; life is not. Hold both at once.
